You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Big Tech’s AI Arms Race: Hundreds of Billions in CapEx Surge, the J-Curve of Returns, and Investment Logic Unpacked

TEXT:
Core Summary
2026 marks the peak year of AI infrastructure investment. The combined CapEx of Microsoft , Amazon , Google ( Alphabet ), and Meta has been revised upward to
$690–745 billion
, a surge of more than 70% year-over-year, with cumulative spending already exceeding $1.1 trillion. Near-term free cash flow is under pressure and the market has grown increasingly sensitive to higher spending guidance, yet the long-term J-curve of returns remains intact — profits are steadily flowing from the model layer into hardware and infrastructure. Because the marginal cost of AI is not zero, the push to squeeze hardware efficiency will continue for a long time . For traders, the most verifiable and high-beta opportunities still lie in the physical bottlenecks: GPUs, advanced packaging, HBM, optical modules, and power & cooling.
I. Scale of the Race: A Historic Infrastructure Wave Still Accelerating
In 2026, the AI arms race among tech giants has reached new heights. The
four companies — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta — have guided combined capital expenditure of approximately
$690–745 billion , up more than 70% from roughly $410 billion in 2025. Recent earnings have further confirmed or raised parts of this guidance:
Amazon: ~$200 billion (largest in absolute terms)
Microsoft: ~$190 billion
Alphabet: raised to $195–205 billion (Q2 actual spend already $44.9 billion, with management explicitly signaling a significant further increase in 2027)
Meta: $125–145 billion (some updates lifted the lower end to around $130 billion)
The bulk of this capital is flowing into high-end AI chips, hyperscale data centers, power and cooling infrastructure, advanced packaging, top talent, and frontier model training.
Nvidia continues to benefit as the core GPU supplier, with its data-center business still growing explosively.
TSMC firmly controls the critical advanced-node process technology and CoWoS advanced packaging capacity.
At the same time, the giants are accelerating in-house chip development (Google’s TPU, Amazon’s Trainium, Meta’s custom silicon) to reduce reliance on any single supplier.
This is no longer merely a hardware contest. It has become a full-spectrum competition spanning infrastructure, models, talent ecosystems, and compute dominance — one of the largest technology infrastructure build-outs in human history. By the end of June 2026, the four companies’ cumulative CapEx since the start of the AI boom had already surpassed $1.1 trillion.
II. The J-Curve of Returns: Long-Term Upside vs. Near-Term Pressure — Profits Flowing from Models to Hardware
The return profile of this massive front-loaded investment clearly exhibits a classic “J-curve”: heavy early outlays, delayed payback, but substantial long-term potential.
Microsoft : Azure growth remains strong (in the 40%+ range) with relatively high AI revenue visibility; free cash flow improvement is expected to lead the group.
Amazon : AWS growth is solid and backlog is ample, yet free cash flow faces the most pronounced pressure in 2026; the majority of returns are expected to materialize in 2027–2028 as new capacity comes online.
Alphabet : Cloud growth is extremely rapid (Q2 Cloud revenue up ~80% year-over-year), but intense investment has already pushed quarterly free cash flow into negative territory; pressure may become more visible around early 2027.
Meta : Returns are captured more indirectly through improved ad targeting and user experience. ROI attribution is relatively opaque, and cash-flow pressure may last longer than peers.
Overall timeline: 2026 is the peak investment and cash-flow stress year. Scaled returns are expected to emerge between 2027 and 2029, depending on data-center utilization rates, AI service pricing power, and enterprise willingness to pay.
Key Insight : The model layer struggles to build lasting network effects and is more likely to compete like a commodity on cost and efficiency. Because the marginal cost of AI is not zero, profits will continue flowing from the model layer into hardware, cloud, and infrastructure. The drive to squeeze hardware efficiency and invest in physical compute will persist for a long time.
III. Diverging Market Sentiment: From “Buying the Narrative” to “Validating Returns”
Market reactions are becoming increasingly polarized:
Bull case : Clear long-term growth trajectory, high order visibility, and expanding platform moats in the AI era. Cloud growth rates and backlogs continue to validate demand.
Bear case : Near-term gross-margin compression, free-cash-flow erosion, rising depreciation burden, and rapid balance-sheet expansion (debt and long-term lease commitments rising sharply). After recent earnings (especially Alphabet’s), the market’s tolerance for higher CapEx guidance has clearly declined, and stock prices have become more sensitive to upward revisions.
Recent results show that free cash flow is no longer the sole metric that matters. Debt leverage — particularly approaching the 1x net-debt credit threshold — and actual utilization rates have become the new focal points. Until those critical leverage thresholds are reached, CapEx is more likely to keep accelerating than to slow down.
IV. Clear Winners and Sectors to Watch
The most transparent beneficiaries remain concentrated in the AI supply chain:
Segment
Key Names
Driver Logic
GPUs & Chip Design
Nvidia, AMD
Explosive data-center demand
Advanced Foundry
TSMC
Monopoly on leading-edge nodes & CoWoS
High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM)
Micron, SK Hynix
Memory bottleneck for AI training
Optical Interconnects / Modules
Marvell, Lumentum
Data-center network upgrades
Servers & Infrastructure
Dell, Super Micro
Hyperscaler capacity expansion
Power & Cooling
Vertiv, Eaton
Energy and thermal constraints
Compared with the cloud platforms themselves, these specialized segments offer stronger cyclical elasticity and higher-beta exposure to the AI infrastructure build-out. A potential buyback narrative in memory (if Micron or SK Hynix deploy a meaningful portion of free cash flow into share repurchases) could also serve as a near-term catalyst.
V. Upcoming Catalysts
Three major catalysts will continue to drive sentiment over the next several quarters:
Subsequent earnings reports: validation of the sustainability of AI hardware demand and actual utilization rates.
Hyperscaler CapEx guidance: whether the intense investment plans are maintained or even raised further.
Infrastructure bottlenecks: progress on power supply, cooling systems, HBM capacity, and advanced packaging.
VI. Trader Playbook: Efficient Participation via Bitget rTokens
Trade rNVDA, rMSFT, rGOOGL, rAMZN, and other 1:1-pegged tokens directly with
USDT .
24/7 markets that respond in real time to news and earnings.
Dividends automatically settled in USDT, with no FX conversion or traditional brokerage account requirements.
Strategy suggestions
Core holdings : Use rTokens to build long-term positions in AI infrastructure leaders (e.g., Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon).
Earnings trading : Tactical entries and exits around quarterly reports to capture volatility.
Supply-chain rotation : During the capacity-expansion phase, rotate into higher-beta suppliers (Micron, Marvell, Dell, power & cooling names, etc.).
Risk management : Combine spot rToken holdings with small futures positions to hedge short-term drawdowns.
Disclaimer : This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. No matter how powerful the AI narrative, disciplined execution remains the ultimate differentiator between winners and losers.
